text.p: Margins for California refiners have rebounded since the start of the year as market players backed off a costly price war to gain gasoline market share, analysts said.
Price cuts at southern California gasoline stations helped push down refining margins in the fourth quarter of 1996 to $4.50 a barrel from $7 in the third quarter.

"Refining margins in California are...showing signs of improvement," said Paul Ting, Salomon Brothers energy analyst, in a weekly refining report. Margins since Jan 1 have climbed to $7.11, a $2 improvement over first quarter 1996, he noted.
The price war, which lasted from late last fall to early March, may have cost oil companies $500 million in lost revenue as they lowered prices to retailers, Ting said.
Atlantic Richfield Co, a top retailer in the state, was a key player in the contest to win customers, analysts said, hoping to increase market share to 23 percent from 18 percent.
"ARCO was certainly the main warrior," said John Vautrain, a consultant with Purvin & Gertz Inc in California.
But ARCO's March 4 agreement to take over 260 gasoline stations owned by Thrifty Oil Co will earn it its desired market share, analysts reckon.
Ting and others say the high cost of the price war make it unlikely another will crop up soon, noting the last significant battle took place in California six years ago.
"I don't think people want to get into a price war easily. It cost them a lot of money," Ting said.
Shell Oil Co ended the war two weeks ago by raising prices eight cents for dealer-tank-wagon gasoline, a wholesale market through which companies supply stations.
California retail gasoline prices have now strengthened from six months ago, fetching an average of seven cents more than other U.S. regions ahead of the main driving season.
"Since we are approaching the summer driving season, we expect refining margins over the next few months to improve over their fourth-quarter 1996 levels," Ting said in his report.
